newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel may hunt "terrorists" in Palestinian areas.
newsitem.headline: Israel may hunt "terrorists" in Palestinian areas.

text.p: Israel vowed on Thursday to re-enter areas it handed over to the Palestinians in order to seize "terrorists" if Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's forces failed to do the job themselves.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's communications adviser David Bar-Illan issued the warning a day after two Islamic suicide bombers killed 13 people in the main Jewish market in Jerusalem and wounded 170.

"The cabinet decision is quite clear. If Israel has to, that is if the Palestinian Authority is not going to do what it is supposed to do against the terrorists, Israel will have to do it," Bar-Illan told Reuters.
"Israel will have to go into the areas controlled by the Palestinian Authority if that is necessary and get the terrorists there," he said.
Late on Wednesday, Netanyahu's security cabinet ordered a halt to peace talks with the Palestinians and demanded that Arafat crack down on Moslem militants who claimed responsibility for the attack.

Israel has handed over much of the Gaza Strip and parts of the West Bank to Arafat's Palestinian Authority under peace deals signed since 1993. It has only rarely re-entered the self-rule areas to make arrests or battle Palestinians.

"The fact is that we must do what we have to do in order to eliminate this scourge and we are just hoping that the peace process will be saved by a total change, a 180-degree change as the prime minister has put it, in the attitude and in the deeds of the Palestinian Authority," Bar-Illan said.

Israeli newspapers published huge photos of men, women and children bloodied by the blast at the Mahane Yehuda market off Jerusalem's main Jaffa Road under such screaming headlines as: "Inferno in the market".
Israel sealed off the West Bank and Gaza Strip and restricted Palestinians to their home districts.
Palestinian cabinet minister Faisal al-Husseini warned Israelis of the repercussions tough actions might have.
"Every punishment against the Palestinian administration strengthens those who are against the peace process," he told Israel's Channel One television.
Eighteen hours after the mid-day blasts, police were still trying to identify the bodies blown apart by the two 10-kg (22 pound) bombs.
Police urged the public to be on the alert for suspicious people and objects. Suicide bombers killed 59 people in a wave of attacks over eight days in February and March 1996.
Police said two bombers detonated bombs in briefcases.
Public Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani said there were signs the explosives might have been assembled in a bomb laboratory uncovered by Palestinian police in June near Bethlehem in the West Bank.
At the market itself, stalls reopened for business after municipal workers spent the night removing debris and cleaning.
Uri Mizrahi, owner of a delicatessen, told Israeli army radio: "I arrived at 5:30. I opened the business as usual. Nothing can break us."

World leaders urged Israel and the Palestinians to press on with negotiations but U.S. special Middle East envoy Dennis Ross postponed a planned mission to salvage peacemaking during a period of national mourning.
A leaflet issued in the name of the Moslem militant Hamas group claimed responsibility. It gave Israel until 1800 GMT on Sunday to free all Palestinian prisoners.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, on her way back from an Asian tour, told reporters Netanyahu had pledged to keep the peace process alive.
She said she was working to renew U.S. aid to Palestinians despite the bombing.
The law making it possible for the United States to deal with and give aid to Arafat's Palestinian Authority expires on August 12 and there has been doubt about whether Congress will extend it.
Israel and the Palestinians agreed this week to resume talks on commitments left over from interim peace accords.
That prompted optimism abroad that negotiations stalled for four months after Israel began building a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem might be back on course.
On Thursday, Israel's former Shin Bet secret security chief Karmi Gillon criticised the decision to halt talks.

"If we're speaking of a suspension of the talks for a very long period, we let terrorism win. In the end it's impossible not to link the attack yesterday to the awakening of the diplomatic process of the last two weeks," he told army radio.

A Palestine Liberation Organisation security official said Arafat, who condemned the bombing, had declared a state of emergency in Palestinian areas and ordered the arrest of activists of "extremist groups" including Hamas and Islamic Jihad.
The bombing was the deadliest since Netanyahu won election in May 1996 on a pledge to bolster security.
